analysis.title: Multi-Asset Perspectives: AI's Rising Fuel Bill (Market Outlook 4Q26)
key_insights: Voya's multi-asset team says AI is a main engine of market returns, but financing costs have risen. Higher rates, energy demand and labor competition make borrowing more expensive for AI companies.

Spending on AI now has to show up as revenue, profit and cash flow. Voya favors self-funded growth, more than one source of earnings and high-quality income while borrowing costs are higher and good news is already priced in.
Long-term U.S. Treasury yields are held up by continued economic growth, deficit financing, higher energy costs and corporate capital raising, including the AI buildout, not only by the Fed.

Voya's leading indicators point to easier inflation ahead. The number of PCE categories above 3% on a 6-month basis is rolling over and wage growth is soft. Voya expects inflation data to look better in 2027.

The U.S. equity advance is narrow. In late September only about half of S&P 500 companies traded above their 200-day moving averages and roughly three-quarters fell during the month, while the largest technology stocks lifted the index.
Expected 3Q26 S&P 500 aggregate earnings growth is 28% (matched companies) versus 8% for the median constituent, so a small group drives much of earnings growth.

Voya would turn more cautious if earnings estimates fell for a sustained period, margins weakened, or large tech showed weaker returns on each new dollar of AI investment, especially if credit conditions tightened at the same time.

Reported backlog and remaining performance obligations for Microsoft ($684bn), Oracle ($664bn), Amazon (~$496bn) and Alphabet ($519.5bn) total about $2.36tn. The report notes these are company-reported measures and may not be comparable.
Voya is constructive on U.S. large caps and neutral on U.S. mid caps, citing potential earnings broadening and healthier balance sheets than small caps.

Voya is underweight U.S. small caps until financing conditions ease and earnings momentum is more durable. Russell 2000 has 66% of debt due in fiscal years 1-5 versus 49% for the Russell 1000, and public bonds are 40% of equity market cap versus 14%.
Voya is neutral on developed international equities with a preference for Japan. Taiwan semiconductors and Korean memory producers depend on the same AI spending cycle as U.S. tech.

Europe is seen as a company-by-company opportunity, with the best case in defense, grid upgrades, energy security and automation. The French-German 10-year spread is 139.5 bp (2011 peak 190.1 bp), and a wider spread could pressure European stocks.

Japan is the preferred developed market outside the U.S. because of better capital use, higher shareholder returns and near-record wage growth. Higher JGB yields and a stronger yen are the main risks for the equity case.

Voya's emerging-market overweight is selective: AI hardware in Taiwan and Korea, domestic demand in India, and commodity or infrastructure beneficiaries. It stays cautious on China's domestic recovery, where exports are strong but consumption is weak.

In fixed income, Voya prefers intermediate Treasuries, agencies and higher-quality credit, with less exposure to the longest maturities. Stock-bond correlation makes bonds a less reliable diversifier. Non-investment grade is limited by tight spreads, and TIPS stay a secondary allocation.
Voya is modestly constructive on the U.S. dollar, supported by resilient U.S. growth, high long-term yields and global demand for dollar funding.
AI exposure also sits in IG credit, REITs (data centers), utilities, infrastructure, commodities and North Asian equities, so portfolios may be less diversified than they look.

Signs the AI engine is straining: weaker AI cash-flow results, wider credit spreads, slower Chinese demand or renewed dollar strength. Cooler inflation and softer labor demand would ease pressure on rates.

sector_views.rationale: Scale, AI demand, earnings power and self-funded growth. Watching margins and the path of earnings estimates.
Potential earnings broadening and healthier balance sheets than small caps. Watching index breadth.
Lower valuations and possible earnings recovery, but refinancing needs, floating-rate debt and higher borrowing costs weigh.
Capital discipline, higher shareholder returns, firmer growth and wage gains. Rates and the yen are the risks.
AI hardware in Taiwan and Korea, India domestic growth and commodity exposure. China domestic weakness and dollar strength are risks.
Defense, grid, automation and energy-security spending offset weak productivity, aging populations, high energy costs and Chinese competition.
Data centers, towers and warehouses offer selected opportunities, but higher long-term yields and refinancing needs weigh.
Intermediate Treasuries, agencies and higher-quality credit provide income, with too much long-maturity exposure a risk.
Targeted inflation protection helps, but high real yields and rate volatility keep the allocation secondary.
Higher yields look appealing, but spreads are tight and refinancing protection is weaker.

earnings_insights: Expected 3Q26 S&P 500 aggregate earnings growth (matched companies) is 28% year over year versus 8% for median constituent net-income growth, per Bloomberg and S&P as of 10/08/26 (493 of 500 companies, estimate not a reported figure).
Voya says analysts expect small-cap earnings to improve, but the proof has not shown up yet.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Below the 2011 peak of 190.1 bp. A wider spread could pressure European stocks.
Exports are strong while domestic demand is weak.

macro_indicators.reading: Categories above 3% on a 6-month basis are gradually rolling over
macro_indicators.interpretation: Voya's leading indicators suggest inflation data will look better in 2027.

risk_factors: Spending growth on AI could slow, and investors may separate companies earning real returns from those that don't.
Narrow market leadership leaves less room for disappointment if AI optimism fades.
Higher long-term yields and refinancing needs weigh on small caps, REITs and non-investment grade credit.
French or Italian yields rising too far relative to German bonds could pressure European stocks.
Higher Japanese bond yields and a stronger yen could hurt Japanese earnings and exporters.
Weak China domestic demand, dollar strength, high Indian valuations and high oil prices are risks for emerging markets.
Stocks and bonds can both fall if inflation, energy prices or heavy government borrowing push rates higher.
Wider credit spreads, weaker AI cash flow, slower Chinese demand or renewed dollar strength would signal strain.

tension_points.bull_case: AI demand is moving from training into everyday use, chip and hardware companies signal steady investment, and large U.S. tech has sales growth, earnings power and cash flow.
tension_points.bear_case: Spending growth could slow, financing costs are higher, and leadership is narrow, leaving less room for disappointment if AI optimism fades.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Sustained falls in earnings estimates, weaker margins, or weaker returns on each new dollar of AI investment, especially alongside tighter credit conditions.

tension_points.bull_case: Lower valuations and analyst expectations for improving earnings.
tension_points.bear_case: More debt, more floating-rate loans, and less room to absorb higher financing costs, with energy and borrowing costs squeezing profits.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Yields and credit spreads would need to stabilize, refinancing would need to get easier, and earnings estimates would need to rise for more than a quarter or two.

theme_stances.key_argument: Higher rates, energy demand and labor competition make AI borrowing more expensive, so spending must show up as revenue, profit and cash flow.
theme_stances.evidence: Every engine requires fuel, and financing costs have increased.

theme_stances.key_argument: A small group of large tech companies drives earnings growth, which leaves less room for disappointment.
theme_stances.evidence: Concentrated leadership can sustain markets for a while

theme_stances.key_argument: Small caps carry more debt and floating-rate loans, so higher financing costs weigh on them.
theme_stances.evidence: We remain underweight small caps until financing conditions ease
